gem_transcription_flat:
BRITISH DRILLING CREWS MAKE GOOD PROGRESS
ON 'SEA GEM'

'Sea Gem', BP's first drilling platform for the North
Sea oil and gas search spudded in on her location 42 miles East
of the Humber on June 5th.

The 5,600 ton platform was towed to her location by two
tugs with a third smaller one in attendance. After being
positioned precisely between four marker buoys her 10 huge legs
were lowered to the sea bed and the deck jacked up 50 feet above
sea level, out of reach of the largest waves.

Forty men crew "Sea Gem". They work in two shifts, 12
hours on and 12 off for 10 days. A third off-duty crew remains
ashore on five days leave. Two-thirds of the men have had
extensive overseas experience of off-shore drilling with BP and
they are the only all-British drilling crews operating in the
North Sea.

O.P.S. The communications room of "Sea Gem" is crammed full
of equipment, including teleprinters and ship-to-shore
radio.

title: A photographic print of Housing, Post War, Houses - Flats, Maisonettes and Estates, etc, including Mews
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Housing Â» Post War Â» Houses - Flats, Maisonettes and Estates, etc, including Mews.
gem_transcription_flat:
should have been heaven, moving from the squalid back-streets of slumland to bright, skyscraper luxury flats, with their constant hot water and built-in central heating. 
 But many young mothers living in the upper storeys are finding it hell. The reason? "We are tied to our toddlers. We must watch them the whole time. We live in constant dread of them getting out of windows, and falling from the balconies." The ground is 180ft. below. 
 The "high-life" mothers put balconies out of bounds, of course. The doors leading to them are kept locked. But windows cannot be locked. 
 Worry 
 Mesh guards on every balcony are essential. And so are playgrounds or day nurseries for "high-life" under-fives, so that they can make friends and play with children of their own age in safety. 
 These suggestions are made in a report "Two to Five in High Flats," published today — the result of a survey of 200 "high-lifers" by mother-of-three, Mrs. Joan Maizels, with help from the Joseph Rowntree Memorial Trust. 
 Mrs. Maizels found that the higher mothers live, the more they worry about their toddlers' safety. 
 And because of the lack of supervised play space, they are "frightened to turn their backs" on their children. 
 The only outings enjoyed by half of the under-fives covered in the survey are to the shops. Their only playground: the flat. 
 One toddler in seven never played with the children of other families, and the general rule was only "occasional visits" to parks and playgrounds. 
 Mrs. Maizels told me yesterday: "Mothers do realise the importance of play to their children. Play is a most necessary part of a toddler's training. His future character depends on his pre-school years." 
 But — what can the mothers do? 
 A small committee supervised Mrs. Maizel's investigations. One of the members, Mrs. Eirene White, M P (Labour, East Flint), said: "Much more is done for young children in other parts of Europe. We would like to see a lot more supervision of play. I'm sure it's not good for mothers and toddlers to be together all the time." 
 "This report shows that many of them are. For three-quarters of the children under five, living above the fifth storey, are never allowed to play alone anywhere but in the flat — with an anxious mother close at hand. 
 That is exactly what I found at the Brandon Estate, Walworth, London, yesterday, where the flats soar 18 storeys high. 
 Auburn-haired Lynn Davies, nearly two, has no friends of her own age, and has no opportunity of ever playing with other children. Her mother, 24-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth Davies, from Yorkshire, hopes that she can soon take Lynn to a nursery school. "She needs the company of other toddlers. She needs adventure in her play. But not danger, of course."

DAY SEVEN . . For five days men have been working
inside and the house is complete.

THERE WERE, at the
latest count, some 120 firms
engaged in the business of
building instant houses, all
without any noticeable in-
stant effect on the housing
lists.
This one is a little differ-
ent. It took just six days
to build and furnish which
may well be a record of
sorts.
But the man who, meta-
phorically speaking, built
the £4,000, centrally-heated
house with all mod. con., is
not shouting too loud just
now. 'It's not unique,' 33-
year-old Mr. John Davies,
managing director of Anvil
Enterprises Ltd., modestly
admitted. 'But we think
we have gone further than
anybody.'
Four men put up the
house in two days on an
exhibition site in Hereford,
just to show it could be
done. Then they spent four
days adding the trimmings,
and on the seventh day they
rested, saw that it was good,
and promptly sold it.
The idea is to do for
private buyers what the
other instant builders are
supposed to be doing for the
councils. Now all that re-
mains is the slight problem
of rustling up an instant
mortgage. . .

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Home + Housing Â» Pre War Only Â» Housing - Slums - London Only.
gem_transcription_flat:
F192/D3/HOUSING/POST WAR SLUMS
---
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
----
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs.May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenites. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T.Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
---

door of their "home".

KENT OATS ARE SPROUTING IN THE STOOK
-----
This farm labourer on a farm at Green Street
Green, near Dartford, Kent, is examining cut oats
which have been out in the weather for the past week
or two - unable to be harvested.
Now, with stooks blown about, grain blown from
the shells, the corn is sprouting where it has fallen
on the ground.
A loss there is, though as yet not serious, but
unless the weather changes quickly this farmer, like
several others who cut their corn some weeks ago, will
find their harvest not worth collecting.

gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/46867

JS THE BIGGEST "WALKING DRAGLINE" IN THE WORLD
31.10.51.
The world's largest "walking dragline" - with a jib 282ft
long and a bucket weighing 22 tons and holding 27 tons of
spoil when full - is now working in the ironstone quarries
of Messrs Stewarts and Lloyds at Corby. Constructed by
Ransomes and Rapiers, Ltd it has taken four years to build,
and it walks under its own power with seven-foot steps.
The dragline is now removing the strata covering the
ironstone bed down to a depth of 100 feet, hoisting the
loaded bucket (a dead weight of about 50 tons) to the
top of the quarry and slews round to deposit the spoil.
Although the [monster] giant machine weighs 1600 tons, and
in its working position is 5 feet taller than Nelson's
Column, it is controlled entirely by one man.
---
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RECEIVED 1 NOV 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
---
COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4
CENTRAL 2266/7.
---

CHILLED BEEF BY AIR 
 HAM.   13.2.59 
 THE FIRST CONSIGNMENT OF CHILLED BEEF EVER TO BE SENT 
 BY AIR FROM CENTRAL AFRICA HAS ARRIVED IN SMITHFIELD 
 FROM SALISBURY, RHODESIA. THE MEAT LEFT SALISBURY 
 ON WEDNESDAY NIGHT AND WAS IN SMITHFIELD LAST NIGHT. 
 THERE WAS [illegible] 1500 POUNDS OF HIND QUARTERS AND IT IS 
 PURELY AN EXPERIMENT TO SEE HOW THE MEAT LASTS ON THE 
 JOURNEY, AND TO FIND OUT IF SUCH A METHOD OF SHIPPING

 CHEAP AIR FREIGHT RATES CAN BE OBTAINED. 
 THE PICTURE SHOWS THE MEAT HANGING IN THE COLD

gem_transcription_flat:
TO WORK with a smile: 84-year-old John Beddow watches one
of his workmates sign on for the day's work.
---
"SONS OF REST" SIGN ON.

GK/7262-1. John Beddow (left) Aged 84, watches as his mate,
Charles Griffiths, aged 73, signs on at 8.30 a.m. Working day
starts at 8.30 and finishes at 5. The men in the main factory
start at 7.30 a.m. and have to clock in. The old workers
appreciate their extra hour in bed in the morning. They work
a five-day week.
---
THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY

GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co, of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

SURPRISE, surprise! The

the Queen's picture on a Christ-
mas card is different.
..

KT/RS.

THE NEW SPACE LOOK AT WOKING.

      The four with the "space-like" look are in fact
demonstrating the very latest in metal spraying
equipment, produced by the METCO company at Chobham,
Woking. The two men on the left are actual sprayers,
while the girls are secretaries with the firm who are
demonstrating the lightness and comfort of the masks.
The main hood is of lightweight fibre glass with an
easily replaceable clear visor, and the weight is
supported by the body instead of the head, making it
practical for it to be worn for long periods. The usual
smell of stale, oil-bearing compressed air experienced
when spraying has been removed by fitting an activated
carbon filter in the air feed line, and a quick-release
connector allows the line to be disconnected so that
the operator can leave the work area without removing
the mask. The size of the mask allows an unusual degree
of movement, and makes it practical for spectacles to
be worn if necessary.

sprayers CLIFFORD WATERSof Maidenhead and ERNEST

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fishing, Accidents - Trawler Losses, January/February 1968 - Families, Demonstrations, etc
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fishing Â» Accidents - Trawler Losses Â» January/February 1968 - Families, Demonstrations, etc.
gem_transcription_flat:
THE COOK of the Ross Cleveland, Bill Howbrigg, aged 59, was taken off the ship last Thursday with pneumonia. After treatment at a hospital in Iceland he was flown home to Hull.
Last night he said: "The weather was dreadful. If it had been up to me I would never have taken a trawler fishing up there.
"The weather was so bad that we had only two days' fishing before I had to leave the ship. Every 12 hours we were out smashing the ice which was making the ship top-heavy.
Axes
"We were using axes, batons, spanners—anything we could lay our hands on. But the weight of ice was forcing the ship down. Sometimes it was impossible to go on deck to clear it.
"We would just get one side cleared, the ship would start to right herself—and then the other side would freeze up. It was murder. If you've never seen it, I can't describe it to you. In weather like this it's like a white hell up there."
Bill, who is unmarried, was talking at the Queen Mary hostel where he lives.
Shocked
He said: "I have been on trawlers since 1926. I would say this weather was as bad as that in which the Lorella and Roderigo were lost 13 years ago.
"But if I am passed medically fit I will still go back to sea.
"I did not want to go to hospital, but the skipper made me go ashore.
"I stayed in hospital until last Friday. All I can say is that I am deeply shocked, but, thank God, I was lucky enough to get out alive."
Bill Howbrigg said the last words spoken to him by the skipper were: "I hope to see you when we get back. Look after yourself."

title: A photographic print of Housing, Post War, Miscellaneous including Moving Houses en Bloc, on wheels, etc
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Housing Â» Post War Â» Miscellaneous including Moving Houses en Bloc, on wheels, etc.
gem_transcription_flat:
PICKED UP any good bargains on the property market lately? One man who has, literally, is Mr. Jack Carmichael, of Long Island, New York.
Our picture shows the old coastguard station he fell in love with being moved lock, stock and chimney pot to its new site.
We in Britain have more ancient buildings to be sentimental about than the Americans, but our hysterical road conditions prevent us from keeping historical buildings intact in this way.
"Streets in the United States are fantastically wide," said a heavy haulage expert at Pickfords.
"Ours are generally so narrow and cluttered by overhead wires that it wouldn't be possible to drive a house through them."
The upper storeys of a 16th-century house were moved last year to be built into a new chain store on the same Hereford site. But the cost was £6,000.
A Cambridgeshire woman had her home dismantled brick by brick to be rebuilt on another site rather than have it bulldozed. This cost £8,000.
Too costly
Costs like these are too high for the average home owner. So the rooms in our homes are doomed to keep their old familiar views.
But in America it is a different story.
The fishing and farming families who live along the far reaches of Eastern Long Island, New York State, would wonder why we find the picture above so remarkable.
For to them, making way for tomorrow without losing yesterday is a commonplace event. There's even a man who "collects" old houses on his shore-line estate and rents them out for the summer.
The coastguard station was going cheap because the land it stood on was needed for a fishing museum.
Mr. Robert Kennelly, who has been moving houses all his working life, explained: "Very often what was once an ideal spot becomes the corner of a new highway or the centre of an industrial complex. Or maybe even some noisy neighbours move in next door.
"So then we get a call to move the house to a new spot. The owner buys a new parcel of land and we move the house for them."
The longest move Mr. Kennelly has done so far has been 60 miles.

NUMBER EIGHT in the
range of pre-fabricated
bungalows is now going up.
It is the Orlit.
Soon after daybreak yester-
day work began on the Minis-
try of Works secret site behind
the Tate Gallery.
By 1.30 p.m. the framework was
up and everything set to put on
the asbestos roof and fill in the
walls. It will be finished some
time to-day.
When I saw the skeleton yester-
day riveters and drills were
clattering away.
At the far end of the secret
“pen” finishing touches were
being put to the Phoenix, design of
the “Mulberry” men.
In between were two other
models still on the secret list—
the Spooner and Universal.
25,000 A Year
Over the other side of a high
wooden fence people were inspect-
ing the original models, the Arcon,
Tarran, Uni-Seco and Portal
Mark II.
Framework of the Orlit is steel
with concrete posts and steel roof
stanchions. Walls are made from
foam slag inside and stone-faced
concrete slabs outside.
Captain C. Ramsden, managing
director of Orlit, Ltd., told me
that production can begin in a
very short time. “I have offered
to turn out 25,000 in 12 months,”
he said.
Late last night lights were burn-
ing in a big office suite in Victoria.
The “Mulberry” men were mak-
ing last-minute changes in the
Phoenix, which the Government
has just adopted.

190146    GAI

PRINCESS ELIZABETH LAYS FOUNDATION OF A NEW CHURCH -
         TO RISE FROM THE BOMB-RUINS.

Bromley, Eng:  It was a great day at this Kentish
town when Princess Elizabeth laid the foundation stone
of the new Parish Church here.
The old church was destroyed by a bomb in 1941, but
the 500-years-old tower was undamaged.  The new church
is to be built onto this.
Cost of the new church will be between £70,000 and
£80,000 - part of which will be paid by the War Damage
compensation, and the rest will come from public appeals.
This was the first time that Bromley had received an
heir to the throne.
PHOTO SHOWS:   With a Guard of Honour of Boy
Scouts, Princess Elizabeth is greeted on her arrival
at the Bromley (Kent) Parish Church, where she laid
the foundation stone.

IRISH NEWS AGENCY COPYRIGHT PHOTO

10.4.52 (8165)
---
IT'S THE WORLD'S BIGGEST PLOUGH
---
NEWBRIDGE, Co. Kildare: It's the largest plough of its type in
the world. It will dig a drain 4 feet deep by 2½ feet wide, and
it has been designed and built at the Newbridge (Co. Kildare)
research station of the Irish Peat Board for use on Irish bogs.
Eugene Gillespie, 38-years-old engineer who conceived this
monster, comes from Gortnahork, Co. Donegal. He is modest about
his achievement. "It's just another plough", he says. Only
reluctantly he admits that when it goes to work, it will dig
the biggest drains in the fastest time yet. The monster took
two months to build - weighs over 1½ tons, has drum
wheels measuring 6 feet by 3 feet 6 ins. and will be drawn
by a tractor. It will be ready for testing in about a fortnight.
If produced commercially, it would cost about £750. When the
plough has been tested and approved, the design will be turned
over to a factory for production. Up to now, the largest
plough used by the Board can cut to a depth of only three feet.
IRISH NEWS AGENCY PHOTO SHOWS: Eugene Gillespie, Irish Peat
Board engineer, with the plough -- largest of its type in the
world -- which he designed for use on Irish bogs. INA
---
RCD. 14 APR 1952

PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS
The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to
the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations and to the
specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B.
It only required three weeks of normal working with a very
small team of men to complete this pair of houses for
occupation. This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time
of any system of truly permanent housing for local authorities
yet developed.
Under this new system, a wide variety of external finishes
to the houses is possible, so avoiding the monotony to which
most industrialised systems and much traditionally built
housing is prone. Internally, room arrangements are extremely
flexible and can be rearranged very quickly and at negligible

title: A photographic print of Industry, Miscellaneous, Unemployed - Post War, 1945
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Miscellaneous Â» Unemployed - Post War 1945.
gem_transcription_flat:
STRANDED EX-CONVICTS FIND A HOME IN A CHURCH
A NEW USE FOR EMPTY PEWS IN KENSINGTON

In the Royal Borough of Kensington there is a church where
every night stranded ex-prisoners and other unfortunate wrecks
of humanity find a place to sleep and call their temporary home.
In the gallery over the pews, and with a view of the altar and
the organ, they roll out their mattresses and get a peaceful
night's sleep, their washing strung out on a line from side to
side of this unusual place of worship. Their stomachs are well
filled with sausage and mash cooked by one of their number in
the church kitchen. No charge is ever made for all this, and
many of them are enabled by thus having an "address" to get
public assistance and then employment - so difficult for a
man with nowhere to go when he leaves his prison after paying
society's price, or for those other men who have fallen on
hard times and for who the Welfare State doesn't cater.
The Rev. Bertram Peake - known in the war as "The Tin Hat
Pastor" - who refused all honours for his work among the blitzed
Londoners, - has found this new use for his old church a
satisfactory continuation of his good, although to some minds,
unorthodox, work of caring for men's bodies as well as souls.
No man is refused at Golborne Church. No charge is made.
Men stay there on average six weeks. For many hope and faith
are renewed, and jobs found before they move on. But there are
always more who come to take their place in the gallery of
comfort in this Kensington Church.
KEYSTONE JP/13740
---
JP/13740-1 THE SERMON BENEATH THE WASHING

The Rev. Bertram Peake preaches from the pulpit of
Golborne Church, Kensington. Before him in the pews are his
"flock", many of them former prisoners. Above him,
not quite hidden, in the gallery, is their washing hanging out
to dry, and their beds. The pulpit was presented to the church
by the brother of a professed Atheist who made this last
bequest to the Rev. Peake when he was dying.
---

BLANDFORD.SUN.28.11.65.
FARM USED AS MARKET.  Story Arnold.
O.P.S. Notices regarding the closure of the market.
---
General view of market.
---
IN these days of quick-dried, deep-frozen, pre-packed foods, the label "Farm-fresh" has an almost magical quality. Everything is certainly farm-fresh at this regular Sunday market — and nearly 500 people turned up yesterday to stock up on eggs, potatoes, butter and cream. Farmers from all over Sussex take their produce to the market which is held in the cowshed on Mrs. Sarah Lloyd-Jones's farm at Buxted, near Uckfield. They shout their wares, joke with the customers and give the whole place the air of a countrified Petticoat Lane. Their favourite spiel is that if you turn up early enough you'll find the eggs still warm from the hen, the milk still bubbling and the brussels still glistening with dew. They like to tell, too, of the man who makes a three-hour train journey from Hounslow, Middlesex, to shop for a whole streetful of people. He didn't show up yesterday. 
 By HARRY ARNOLD 
 Picture by LEN BLANDFORD 
 But people did come from 50 miles around, turning the thing into a jolly country fair. The farmers started it as a protest against the price review. They sell at average prices but make more profit with no middlemen or retailer to pay. But the market has proved too successful. And Uckfield Rural Council have issued a closing order. They have never liked the enterprise and chairman Stewart Mac-Kinney, a farmer himself, yesterday explained why. The council, he said, claim the market is unnecessary and is held on agricultural land. Parking facilities are inadequate and traffic congestion is caused in the village every Sunday. At the door of her cowshed, Mrs. Lloyd-Jones, chairman of the local committee of the National Farmers' Union, talked of an appeal against the closure order, backed by a petition from the customers. "No one," she said, "has the right to stop us giving this service. We do not sell at cut-prices." She added: "The reason we are popular is simply that everything is farm-fresh." And at the end of the day there was £600 in the tills to prove it.

1983 - 5236 / 14343
---
Igloo-shaped home out of reinforced paper

P APER HOUSES are no longer just a flimsy idea. Prototypes, produced by the London firm of Tri-Wall Containers Ltd., have finished final tests and models should be on the market next year.
The temporary houses are one-storey, igloo-shaped units made from a very tough reinforced paper called corrugated fibre board.
They can be weatherproofed against most climatic conditions and will last for at least a year.
Building them can be very quick. A team of four men can put up a paper house in three hours—and demolish it in minutes.
Originally designed for emergency use in disaster areas, the houses are built by stapling together identical fibre board panels into hexagonal shapes.
Each panel supports another so that when they are all in place the houses stand firmly without any other help.
Larger buildings for use as schools and hospitals can be made by leaving out panels in a number of units and joining them all together into circular blocks.
Single living units have a door with adjoining glass window at the front and rear. They stand 10ft. high at the centre peak and have a 20ft. wide floor space. Plumbing and electricity can be installed normally.
Apart from disaster relief, the houses can also be used for workmen on isolated building sites. And in some cases they can even be cemented on the outside to become semi-permanent.
The price of a paper house has not yet been worked out, but Tri-Wall expect it to be in the region of £150.

MAKING THE CORONATION CARPET ON THE LARGEST
LOOMS IN SCOTLAND. 10.3.37.
The carpet that is to be laid in Westminster Abbey for
the Coronation ceremony is now being carefully made in a Glas-
gow mill. The carpet has several special features. It is one
of the biggest ever made, the pieces, of which there are many,
are 40ft. x 35ft. and the surface is getting special treatment
to make it as smooth as glass, this has been found necessary to
allow the flowing trains of the royal ladies and peeresses who
will walk on it, an easy passage, as any minute obstruction would
catch in the frail material they will wear. The carpet, owing
to its gigantic size, is being made on the largest looms in
Scotland, of messrs. TEMPLETON of Glasgow, who also made the
Coronation carpet for George V when he was crowned in 1912. The
Scots girls who are now working on the carpet, feel delighted
to be sharing in the work for this historic ceremony and are
taking extra special care at all stages of progress to produce
the finest example of carpet making.
O.P.S. Some idea of the size of the pieces can be gathered from
this row of girls working on the loom that is making the
carpet. HHS/B, KEYSTONE.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S DAILIES.....NOV.26th '56.

SEARCHING FOR OIL IN BRITISH WATERS.
                                      26.11.56.
The first water-borne geophysical survey to be carried
out by the British Petroleum Oil Company of the British
Coast took place recently, in the 1000 ton converted corvette
"SEISLIM", the first British-owned vessel to be specially equipped
for this work, off Swanage and Lulworth Cove. The purpose was
to investiaget the nature of the rocks beneath the sea bed
at 10,000 ft. B.P. has been carrying out a search for oil-
bearing rock formations in the British Isles for [strikeout] 21
years and this was its latest effort.
Charges were exploded four and half feet below the surface
of the water, along a previus plotted line. Vibrations
transmitted into the sea bed and reflected back from various
rock formations were picked up by detectors towed behind the
ship. They were then record electrically on a time chart
which is afterwards analysed by experts at The British
Petroleum Compnay's London Office.
                         Picture shows
Floating cable with geophones mounted on paravanes stored
on deck on completion of day's operations. E.K. LOVELOCK is
handling a geophone assembly.

THE BIGGEST "WALKING DRAGLINE" IN THE WORLD
JS                                       31.10.51.
The world's largest "walking Dragline" - with a jib 282 feet long
and a bucket weighing 22 tons and holding nearly 27 tons of
spoil when full - is now working in the ironstone quarries of
Messrs Stewarts and Lloyds at CORBY. Constructed by Ransomes and
Rapiers, Ltd it has taken four years to build and walks under its
own power taking seven-foot steps. The dragline is now removing
the strata covering the ironstone bed down to a depth of 100 ft,
hoisting the loaded bucket (a deadweight of about 50 tons) to
the top of the quarry, and slewing round to deposit the spoil.
Although the giant machine weighs 1600 tons, and in its working
position is 5ft taller than Nelson's Column, it is controlled
entirely by one man.
     The picture shows a view inside the main machinery
cabin where the 14 motors provide a total of 3,150 h.p.

Silk for the Queen's Coronation robe
is likely to come from Zoe Lady Hart
Dyke's silkworm farm at Lullingstone
Castle, Eynsford, Kent, where this
picture has just been taken. Lady
Hart Dyke wrote to the Queen offering

would be pleased if the silk for her

Lullingstone silk farm. As yet, no
detailed arrangements have been made.
Lullingstone silk was used in the
Coronation robes of the Queen Mother
and two Princesses at the King's

Queen's wedding dress.
Lady Hart Dyke started breeding
silkworms at her Lullingstone Castle
home in 1934.

cocoons at Lullingstone silk farm.

REVIVING THE DYING ART OF WIG-MAKING

The free supply of wigs under the National Health
scheme has increased the demand for them and brought
to light the problem of lack of labour in this trade.
A craft which requires patience, skill and painstaking
application, it does not attract young people, who can
earn more elsewhere, and so most of the wig-makers are
elderly people. Wigs are made from women's hair, costing
as much as five pounds an ounce, and the hair is knotted
2 or 3 strands at a time onto a foundation of French
silk net. Infinite care is then required to achieve the
correct shape and the necessary shade to give the hair
the necessary semblance of authentic growth.

INP PHOTO SHOWS: Miss Eleanor Jackson, one of the
workers at Wig Creations, Ltd., London,
damps the hair of a newly made wig,
after which it will be set to the
required style and placed in a drying
cabinet.

A FAMILY OF GLASS-EYE MAKERS.

Glass-eye making is an art handed down from father to son
for the last 150 years in the family of Mrs.Taylor, of
New Oxford Street in London. The Duke of Wellington was
one of the first distinguished customers of the firm, and
they still keep two of his artificial eyes in a little
museum - he had his artificial eyes renewed every year.
To-day, the actual production lies in the hands of Mr.
Godfrey Taylor, a young man of 22, who can make a perfect
glass eye within 30 minutes. His mother and his 24-year-
old sister Molly run the business side of their undertaking,
but they, too, are trained to 'make eyes' and can well
replace Godfrey should he be prevented from working.

FLATS DISASTER.

1968 . 1243 : D (6)
---
We'll never go back, say families
Once they had a home . . now all they have left are possessions
AN EMERGENCY centre was set up to house families made homeless by the collapse.
People living nearby arrived with pramloads of clothes and blankets.
But last night nearly all families had been temporarily housed with friends and relations.
Mr. Frederick Davies, Newham's Housing Manager, said: "We have been overwhelmed by offers and we do not think we will need to use the emergency centre which has been set up at Canning Town library.
He said nearby boroughs had offered to begin today looking for temporary accommodation for any of the homeless who needed it.
Earlier, some of the shaken families were allowed to collect their belongings from parts of the block which were considered safe.
Mr. John White came out of the building clutching his cat Tim. He said: "It mattered a lot to me to get Timmy."
Many of the families who escaped the crash have said they will not live in the flats again.
Mother-of-three Mrs. Iris Morgan said: "I could never go back."
And Mr. Alan Smith said: "Next time it will have to be a house or maisonette - no matter how long it takes."

WHERE THE BATS OF THE GREAT TAKE SHAPE

In a small corrugated iron hut in West St., Sutton,
Surrey, where Montague Odd, who died last June, made
cricket bats for W.G. Grace, his two sons, Alec and
Philip carry on the family tradition of craftsmanship.
Most of the delicate job is done by hand, the only
machinery being a wood lathe and binder for the handles.
The clefts of willow which will one day sent the ball to
the boundary, come from Essex, Surrey and Norfolk, and
are hung to be 'cured' for some 4 to 6 months, during
which time they lose about two pounds in moisture. The
cane for the spring comes from Sarawak or Manila, and
the shaping to size balance and shape are done with the
help of experienced hand and eye.

PHOTO SHOWS: Alec Odd weighing a finished bat in the
little workshop in Sutton.

BRITISH MINT WORKS OVERTIME -
169716.(LUD). TO PROVIDE MORE CHANGE FOR WORKERS.

LONDON, ENG: Because of a scarcity of change, workers at
the Royal Mint, here, are being increased from 800 to 1,000-
working day and night in twelve-hour shifts.
With over £127,000,000 worth of coins in circulation -
double the amount in 1939 - firms often find difficulty
in filling pay packets with the correct amount. The momentary
shortage is an apparant mystery - but hoarding is blamed
for some of it.
The Royal Mint, the Government office where British money
is coined, stands on Tower Hill, and was erected in the
year 1810. The nominal head is the Chancellor of the
Exchequer, but the actual chief is the deputy Master, a
civil servant who is appointed by the First Treasury Lord.
Besides all money in circulation in England, all medals
awarded by the Crown are made at the Royal Mint, and certain
Colonies are supplied with silver and bronze coins directly
from this department.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Operators at the Royal Mint examining
finished coins on a special overlooking machine, provided
with moving canvas belts, during the process of making
more coins for circulation.
May, 1948. PN-s. (List - I.)
---

SAFETY IN MINES RESEARCH STATION.         WS/C

In a little colony of low lying buildings on a bleak
hilltop at Harpurhill, Derbyshire, a handfull of men are
fighting continually against the causes of coalmine disasters
Coal dust, under certain conditions is as dangerous as high
explosive and these men are experimenting every day to find
an effective emthod of combating the menace.  A four foot
wide tube to represent a mine shaft is filled with coal dust
and purposely exploded, then the burnt out dust known as
(after damp) a very poisonous gas, is analysed.  More deaths
are caused by the gas than the actual explosion.

Photo shows-  The explosion taking place, watched intently
by the men.
FOX. MAY 4th. 36.
---
I N a depression at the foot of a slope on
the Derbyshire moors, a few miles from
Buxton, two great black pipes, resem-
bling huge water-mains, stretch out for
half a mile.  These are the
experimental galleries in which
coal dust explosions are created.
Pit props and timbers are placed
inside, and pulverised coal is
scattered along the road.
A cartridge is fired by elec-
tricity, and with a bang a cloud
of dust bursts out at the end of
the gallery, to explode into a
great flame, after which the
deadly brownish clouds of car-
bon monoxide come rolling out
of the tunnel, while the props
and timbers, after travelling for
half a mile through the gallery,
may be hurled a hundred yards
or so from the mouth.

1983-5236/41387
---
FARM OR FACTORY? BROILER BUSINESS SETS A PROBLEM

THE RAPIDLY EXPANDING BROILER BUSINESS
WHICH HAS BROUGHT MILLIONS OF CHICKENS TO THE
BRITISH HOUSEWIFE IS CAUSING A PROBLEM FOR THE
MINISTRY OF HOUSING - FOR AT THE MOMENT THEY DO
NOT NEED PLANNING PERMISSION.
FARMERS ALL OVER THE COUNTRY HAVE ERECTED
MODERN SINGLE STOREY BUILDINGS TO HOUSE THOUSANDS
OF CHICKENS - ALL WITH AUTOMATIC HEATING, VENTILATION,
WATERING AND FEEDING.
THERE IS ALSO THE PROBLEM OF RATING WHICH,
AT THE MOMENT, IS ALSO CAUSING A PROBLEM - BECAUSE
THE FARMER IS INSISTENT THAT IT IS A FARM - BUT
LOCAL AUTHORITIES ARE MORE INCLINED TO TAKE THE VIEW
THAT IT IS A FACTORY.
THE MINISTER IS NOW CONSULTING LOCAL
AUTHORITIES AND FARMING INTERESTS TO SEE IF ANY
ACTION IS NECESSARY.
HOWEVER, ONE LOCAL AUTHORITY HAS ALREADY
REFUSED TO DE-RATE HATCHERY PREMISES AND BROILER
HOUSES - AT HUNTINGDON. THEY PROVED THAT THE RUNNING
OF A BUILDING CONTAINING BIRDS WAS NOT SUFFICIENT
TO ESTABLISH A RIGHTFUL CLAIM (AS A FARMER FOR THE
LOWER RATING). IT APPEARS THAT THE PLANNING
AUTHORITIES ARE ALIVE TO THE UGLINESS OF SOME OF
THE BROILER HOUSES - SOME OF THEM 200 FEET LONG -
WHICH ARE BUILT ON LAND WHICH IN ITSELF IS NOT USED
FOR FARMING.
PICTURE SHOWS:

THE INTERIOR OF A MODERN BROILER HOUSE. THE BIRDS
ENTER IT AT TWO TO THREE WEEKS AND EMERGE FIVE OR
SIX WEEKS LATER FOR THE TABLE.
DURING THAT TIME THEY HAVE BEEN FED, WATERED,
AND HOUSED IN A WARM VENTILATED ATMOSPHERE BUT IN
VERY SUBDUED LIGHT.
82704 20/10/59 JOHN TOPHAM
---
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
21 OCT 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
---
INDUS-AGRIC-POULTRY + FARMS

LUXURY FLATS.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Housing Â» Post War Â» Accidents.

---
JOHN FREWER, 7

---
DAILY

14 JUL 1961
PLEASE RETURN TO
ART LIBRARY
---
Two of the boys who escaped . . seven-year-old John Frewer, left, and
Billy Cox, centre, with their friends.
---
A NINE-YEAR-OLD boy was killed and five other boys were injured last night when the roof of a derelict house caved in.

The boys were trapped under girders and piles of bricks and wood before rescuers managed to free them.

Mothers of the boys and men from a public house near the building, clawed at the debris with their bare hands.

Firemen with flame-cutting apparatus worked stripped to the waist.

The boy who died in the three-storey house in Anthony-street, Stepney, was Robbie Jitterbo.

Four of the injured boys were detained in London Hospital.

They are Robby Hatton, aged nine (face, head and neck injuries), and Michael Meah, aged 10 (leg and face injuries), both of Montefiore House, Cannon Street-road, Stepney; Tommy McLaughlin, aged 14 (head injuries), of Anthony-street, Stepney, and Nino Casser, 12, (back and leg injuries), of Cannon Street-road.

William McLaughlin, Tommy's 12-year-old brother, was treated in hospital, but went home later.

He crashed through their "den" in the building. They were playing on the roof 40ft. up trying to reach the branches of a pear tree.

One boy who escaped before the house caved in was Michael Shields, aged 13, of Montefiore House.

He said later: "I was swinging on a branch of the tree trying to pull it down when the roof collapsed.

"I was left hanging 15 feet up.

"I jumped down to see if I could get the other boys out. But I couldn't.

"So I ran to a telephone box and told the police to come very fast because some boys were trapped."

Mrs. Catherine McLaughlin, aged 52, mother of Thomas and William, said she heard a crash and screams and saw the building falling.

She added: "I sprang across the road. Through a cloud of dust I could see tons of wreckage piled up in front of me.

"I realised both my boys must be trapped."

Eleven-year-old David Meah saved the life of his 10-year-old brother, Mike.

David said: "I saw Mike's leg sticking out from a heap of bricks. I ran over and started to lift the bricks from his body."
---

gem_transcription_flat:
“HALF HOUR FREE FOR THE
GOVERNMENT WE CHOSE”

SEVENTY builders on Bexley Council's housing site at Westwood-lane, Welling, Kent—already working nine hours a day—yesterday worked an extra half-hour, without pay.
They were carrying out the pledge they made on Wednesday, to help Mr. Aneurin Bevan's drive for 30,000 more homes by Christmas, and they will go on until the block of houses they are working on is finished.
Said one of them: “We reckon the Labour Government we elected will stand or fall on its housing policy, and we are going to do our level best to see that it stands.”
Because the union agreement only allows them to work one hour's paid overtime a day—which they are already doing—they decided to work the extra 30 minutes for nothing—clocking in 15 minutes early in the morning, and cutting the lunch hour by 15 minutes.
Mr. C. J. Pepper, the council's building superintendent, who came in an hour early yesterday, said:
“We hope to have the first house on the site ready for occupation in three weeks. It will go to the first family on our priority list, which now numbers well over 4,000 names.”

---
DAILY HERALD
Copyright
Photograph

NUMBER...........
---
The showrooms . . there were still customers, but no sales
In the showroom window, notices still advertised a "continuous demonstration" of the firm's latest washing-machine.
Customers were still turning up. Still wanting to buy. Still convinced that nowhere else would they find such value.
One housewife travelled 20 miles to get a refrigerator. "It doesn't make any difference to me," she said. "I don't care what's happened. I want one."
She went home, however, without one. No one was selling. The showroom stayed closed.
"It's a shame," said one salesman. "We could sell lots. Customers are scrambling to get machines while they can."
But as the afternoon wore on the confidence of the men still waiting outside began to fade.
To vanish with the news that there was to be no fight. That this was the end.
The salesmen, despondent but even then half-disbelieving, held a meeting. And pulled out £1 notes to pay for a solicitor to look after their rights.
They claimed the firm owes them about £150 each in wages and retention money—a sum held in security against the stock they carry.
But not all could so easily give up hope. Salesman Bill Taylor, of Luton, stayed optimistic to the end.
He paid £20 in cash for a friend's £40 Rolls Razor cheque. Because, he said, "I know I'm still on a winner."

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Motor Â» Factory Scenes - Miscellaneous.
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/52190
---
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS  18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.
Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 1 1/2 hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced 1/4-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.
---
DAILY HERALD
ART LIBRARY
RETURNED UNDAMAGED

London, Eng:- To preserve the knowledge of gold coining,
which has been handed down from craftsmen to craftsmen,
a small coinage of 100,000 sovereigns has been struck
at the Royal Mint here. They will not be for issue.
They were struck from the dies used for the 1925 issue.
(This 1925 issue was struck to replace light-weight coins
in the stock of the Bank of England. The general issue
of gold coinage was suspended in 1917). - Therefore the
issue which has just been struck bears the head of King
George V.
Further small mintings will take place in the future, but
again, only for the purpose of preserving the gold coining
craft.

HE long, deep shop in the works, vast and dim,
where steel is made, where rows of furnaces
pour out their streams of running metal—this
is the heart of Sheffield, town of steel.
Before one of the furnaces stands a man whose name
is Steel. Fred Steel, first furnace hand, whose job is
one of the fiercest, most gruelling in the world. On the
left is his portrait taken in the light of his own fires.
He and his workmate had advanced before the opened
mouth of the furnace and with their twenty-foot irons
had just stilled the boiling steel. At furnace heart the
temperature reaches 1,670 degrees centigrade.
Fred Steel steps back, pushes his blue glasses from

Neighbours of Mr and Mrs P.J. Munro of Oxberry Avenue,
Fulham, can watch ship-building in progress  by looking
out of their back windows.  Mr. Munro, production

finished, the craft will be lifted into the lane at the

ESTEN   D.H.   1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years.  Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet.  He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1  70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge

---
"SQUATTERS" TAKE OVER AT REGENT'S PARK
---------------------------------------
22-8-46

"SQUATTERS" have moved into an Anti-Aircraft gun
site at Primrose Hill, near Regent's Park, London.
These huts were originally intended for Polish
soldiers and their wives, but the inevitable
squatters have now taken over. They are homeless people
who take the possession of empty army huts, gun sites
etc. without waiting for any official decision about
the future of the disused military camps. The movement
has spread recently all over Britain, and a deputation
of squatters went to Whitehall to ask the Government to
clarify their legal position.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:        Mr. and Mrs. C. CLARKE and
                           family, and Mr. and Mrs. J.

condemned house at Chalk Farm, now have neighbouring huts,
but for the present they are feeding communally until they
are really settled in.

JAGUAR LEADS THE WORLD WITH THE NEW E-TYPE: PRODUCTION STEPPED
UP BY 50%
Presenting the new E-type Jaguar - the car that's put
Britain ahead on the road, rocketed her dollar earning exports,
and is fast becoming the latest status symbol for up-and-comers
with an eye for a jazzy means of transport.
The brain behind the E-type is Mr. William Heynes, chief
engineer who joined Jaguar boss Sir William Lyons' Coventry
team in 1935. His new design is revolutionary - built up largely
from the racing Jag - but Mr. Heynes has, with some conservatism
and some criticism, retained the old Jaguar gear box.
A rush of orders was expected, but Sir William didn't
bargain for the need to step up production by 50%. Down in the
Coventry works extra night shifts are being put on to cope with
demand.
And even though buyers in this country will probably
have to wait about a year for a new model, orders still pour in
from discerning motorists for this super sports car that looks
good, moves fast - top speed is 150mph - and only costs just
over £2000.

XML)   INAUGURATION OF EUROPE'S LARGEST FORGING
        PRESS FOR ALUMINIUM ALLOY

Europe's newest and largest forging press for aluminium
alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High	Duty Alloys, Ltd., by
the Chairman, Sir Frank Spriggs.  Known as "Goliath,"
this 12,000-ton press, the first of its type in Great
Britain, has been designed to give working pressures of
4,000, 8,000 and 12,000 tons.  The press itself weighs
800 tons and has an overall height of 56ft. 4in.  Of
this, 42ft 9in. is above ground level and the remainder
with the hydraulic system for operating the movable
table, is concealed below ground level.  It cost more
then £500,000.

THE FOOD and Wine
Society, together with
the Farm Produce
Council, organised a
taste-in yesterday. Wine
and apples.
There were seven wines
and nine varieties of
apples. Combinations of
each amounted to 63
separate tastings. No one,
however, appeared to take
the risk.
There was more than an
outside chance of getting
stomach ache and failing a
breathalyser test, all at
the same time.
Piled up
The apples were brought
up from Tunbridge Wells
by Mr. Ben Tompsett,
chairman of the National
Farmers' Union Kent Fruit
Committee, and piled on
dishes next to chateau-
bottled Sauternes.
There were Laxtons and
Cox's and Lord Lam-
bourns, Russets and Alling-
ton Pippins.
Among the wines to be
tried with them were a
1940 Chateau Latour
Blanc, 1939 Chateau de
Rayne and a 1949 Chateau
Rabaud.
Not all of them mixed.
Several members of the
society suffered acute
withdrawal symptoms
after the third or fourth
slice of apple.
Others, however, were
more enthusiastic. The
idea, said Mr. Claude
Morny, secretary of the
Wine and Food Society,
was to remind members of
the different varieties, and
the subtleties of taste, of
English apples.
"But I'm not suggesting
that anyone should choose
a wine merely to suit a
particular desert apple," he
added.
Afterwards Mr. Tompsett
enthused: "I have been
staggered by the know-
ledge about apples which
has been displayed here to-
night. Unfortunately, I
had little chance to taste
the wine."
---
N

1955-1093-1

Family in cellar get
a house
at last
By Betty Crisp
I WENT underground at Torquay yesterday to the two rooms and a cupboard where a family of six has lived for five years "under the pavements."
The Torquay cave dwellers were happy.
They had just heard that they would get the first council house available, instead of waiting till November as the Housing ommitCtee proposed.
Mother-Mrs. Doris Potter, aged 40-telephoned eldest daughter, Jean, 20-year-old shop assistant, with the good news.
Then she went off to tell father-Mr. Tim Potter, aged 47-a chef at a holiday camp.
Pauline, 11, and Ron, nine, jumped with joy when they returned from school and heard they would soon have a proper place to keep their two pet hamsters. And Anne, 14, at the technical college, could hardly believe that she and Jean would soon have their own bedroom.
I saw the bedroom they have shared with their parents and the younger children at Wellesley-road, for five years.
Three beds
The 14ft. by 11ft. room was crammed with a single and two double beds, a wardrobe and two chests of drawers.
But the furniture could only be seen when the light was on, for this is the room Mr. Gibbings said only got light from "a grating in the pavement."
There is a wall up to street level a few inches in front of the only window with iron bars on top.
The rain splashes in, for both window and the door into the sitting-room have to be kept open in all weathers so that the Potters can breathe.
The Council was told: "It is hardly fitting that the Queen of the English Riviera (Torquay's advertising slogan) should house a family of four children in what you can practically describe as cellars."
No window
The Potters' sitting-room, 14ft. by 12ft., has a normal window opening on to the sloping ground at the back of the house. Their third "room" is a cupboard under the basement stairs, once the coal hole, where Tim Potter has fitted a gas cooker and a sink.
There is no window, or ventilation, and not enough spare space to swing a mouse.
"I can hardly believe we are going to get a council house at last," said Jean, a pretty auburn-haired girl.
"Mum and Dad were on the Torquay list years ago. Then they had to go to Birmingham to work and when they came back in May, 1950, they were told they must go on the bottom of the list again and wait five years.
"It has been so awful having no privacy, especially as we children grow older. Fancy Anne and myself with our own bedroom. A real one with a window that lets in sun and air."
DAILY HERALD July 7 1955 3
---

ERECTING KENT'S FIRST ALUMINIUM SCHOOL
Ods 12.4.49.
The first of the five schools to be built by the Kent County Council
in aluminium prefabricated sections, is now well under way. The
school will be known as the Grays Farm County Primary School, and
is at St. Paul's Cray. The walls and roofs are of aluminium alloy
in prefabricated sections supplied by the Bristol Aeroplane (housing)
Company, and they are delivered to the site ready for erection. Thus
much time and labour, apart from materials, are saved. The block
illustrated in these pictures will house five classrooms and one
general purpose room. There will be another block housing two
classrooms and a general purpose room, an administrative wing,
assembly hall, canteen kitchen, dining hall, etc., and the whole
school will accommodate 360 children. The only brickwork will be
the external gable end walls and the boiler house, the foundations
of which can be seen in some of the pictures, which were taken
during a visit to the site today.

examining every one of the thousands of links in

All production employees of the Austin Motor Company's works -
14,800 in all - are affected by a shut-down of the factories caused
by the coal shortage.  Stocks of fuel are said to be so low that
it will be impossible to start work again unless the present
allocation is revised and delivery increased, and the works may be
closed for several weeks.
With coal distribution crippled by blizzards, hundreds of industrial
plants throughout Britain have had to close down temporarily, and many
thousands of workers have been thrown out of work.

at Longbridge, Birmingham, looking up at a "fuel thermometer" notice

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, Jan 21st.
"QUEEN ELIZABETH" OF THE AIR TAKE SHAPE
21.1.47.
In the early summer it is hoped that the Bristol "Brabazon" pro-
totype of Britain's largest airplane, will make her first flight.
Work on the giant aircraft began just over a year ago, and her
construction will have involved an outlay of £4,000,000, the
destruction of a village and a golf course, and the building of
a special runway costing £2,000,000.
She will be 177ft long with a wing span of 230ft (30ft longer than
the distance between the main structures of Tower Bridge), and
weigh 130 tons, and eight Centaurus gas-turbines of 2500 hp each
will power her. "Brabazon's" later models will carry 100 passengers
in comfort at 250 mph on Britain's Atlantic services.
In this picture what looks like the framework of a prefabricated
house is an outer wing section of the "Brabazon" in which engineers
will have access to the turbines during flight just as they do in
a surface ship. In the background nestling in a steel cradle, and
surrounded by scaffolding and platforms, is the massive fuselage.
---
22 JAN 1947
---

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Aircraft Â» Brabazon - Construction Â» Post-War.
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/42277
---
126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the ' Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I',
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort.  The 143-foot
cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent cabin
altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 feet.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 foot - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the height
over the rudder is 50 foot.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve, air-cooled
radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower for
take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 foot, an economical cruising speed
of 250 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles.  Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 foot,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The sleek nose of the Brabazon's hull
in the construction shop at Filton.
AND March 31st 1947 PN.r.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, August 20th.

HARVESTING ON THE SUSSE "PRAIRIES"
20.8.47.
The present crisis has brought about the biggest Government drive
for a great increase in the production of home-grown food, and
the Prime Minister has called for a £100,000,000 step-up in this
direction by 1950-51. Since the War Office handed back, a year
ago, many acres of land which had been used for Artillery
training purposes, the East Sussex War Agricultural Committee had
been responsible for over a 1,000 acres [illegible] of corn being
grown. This is now in process of being harvested, and in this
picture, one of the biggest single "fields" in the country,
stretching for more than 200 acres across the rolling Sussex
Downs, is being harvested of its corn. The binders are starting

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II, Royal Variety Show, October, 1962
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Queen Elizabeth II Â» Royal Variety Show Â» October, 1962.
gem_transcription_flat:
After the show, the stars line up to meet the Queen. They are from right: Bob Hope, Sophie Tucker, her pianist Ted Shapiro and Edie Adams
---
THE world and Bernard
Delfont breathed again
yesterday. Not only was
peace saved but the Royal
Variety Show was able to
go on without the cuts
Delfont would have had to
make if the international
situation had worsened.
Bob Hope was able to include
the bit where he says: "And
then came the war," with
searchlights darting across the
stage and explosions in the
wings.
Harry Secombe, Norman
Vaughan and Terry Kendall did
their mock march as Sandhurst
cadets.
CLEAN-UP
And, above all, Edmundo Ros was
able to play the signature tune
that he has had for 22 years since
the band first started in the dark
days of 1940-the Cuban Love
Song!
Mr. Delfont who, with Leslie A.
MacDonell presented the show, was
busy during rehearsals all the
same, cleaning up a little in places.
Among those he had a quiet word
with were Mike and Bernie
Winters, Dickie Henderson,
Norman Vaughan and Sophie
Tucker.
Nothing scandalous, mind you,
a word here, a gesture there.
"Very funny, but OUT," said Mr.
Delfont.
Brimming with hokum, laced
with sentiment, the best of what's
left of variety went on at the
Palladium undimmed.
And next Sunday, the television
audience can join the Queen,
Prince Philip and those of her
subjects who were last night able
to afford anything from one to 20
guineas for a ticket.
They will see Harry Secombe,
magnificent in Canadian Mountie
uniform, sing a duet from Rose
Marie, with Eartha Kitt; they will
see Eartha Kitt draping 15ft. of
chinchilla fur around her neck to
sing I'm Just An Old-fashioned
Girl; and Bob Hope telling Edie
Adams that this week the Chang-
ing of the Guard is being done
outside the American Embassy.
INCOMPARABLE
But most of all, and best of
all, they will see the incomparable
Sophie Tucker, resplendent in
silver-blue gown with matching
mink, singing her life story.
Every word came out clear as a
cannon in that husky, red-hot-
momma voice that told the saga of
Sophie in 11 minutes of command-
ing presence, sly humour, perfect
timing, and noble womanhood—
even if she is 74.
SPECTACLES
There were other moments, too—
Dickie Henderson's fooling, Cliff
Richard, introduced by his group
The Shadows as "our vocalist," the
splendid Johnny Dankworth band
with the equally splendid Cleo
Laine—who after a false start
("just nerves") gave one of the
smoothest performances of the
evening.
And the spectacles—The Black
and White Minstrels closing the
first half in a riot of pink and
white plumes and the Edmundo
Ros orchestra and dancers opening
the second with a whirl of Latin-
American rhythm.

gem_transcription_flat:

---
9 - AUG 1946
---
MORE FURNITURE GOES INTO ARMY HUTS DESPITE QUIT NOTICES.

A policy of 'sit tight' and await developments has been adopted
by ex Servicemen who, with their wives and children, have moved
into unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire, because they were unable to find other
accommodation as a result of the housing shortage. Notices to
quit have been served on some of the 'squatters', and German
prisoners have been brought in by the military authorities to
start pulling down huts on the site scheduled for demolition.
Among the families installed are Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines
and their 3 1/2-year-old daughter Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an
inspector in a Diesel factory, is a former Petty Officer in the
Navy who won the British Empire Medal for bringing a lifeboat
safely to land after it had been 39 days in the Atlantic following
the torpedoing of a troopship. While recovering from his ordeal
in New York he met Caroline - now his wife, who comes from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mrs. Caroline Vines (second from right) assisted
by Mrs. Helen Holmes (on right), also in occupation of a hut, and
the children of other neighbours as she moves furniture into one
of the Nissen huts.
LUD August 9th 1946 PN.r.

game have started work in a new job selling men's shirts to
retailers. They are the first of a team to be taken on by
Cornes and Company, 18, Finsbury Circus, London, E.C.2.
The girls have been fitted out for their parts as
commercial travellers and their appearance in the City is
expected to cause much comment.
From the left they are, Jean Radcliffe (19) of Watford
Way, Mill Hill; Anne Marchmont (21) of Upper Richmond Road, Sheen,
and Rosemary Dewhurst (19) of Sherwood Park Road, Mitcham.
All the girls have worked in the drapery trade.
They will also meet buyers at a party where the non-
creasing character of the product will be demonstrated by one of
the world's best exponents of Judo.
As an experiment which has never been tried before, the
venture is seen by Cornes & Co., as a new approach to selling.
"Many women have more tact and business ability than
men. If we find the experiment works as we think it will, more
girls will be taken on in other parts of the country," said
Leonard Steel, a director of Cornes.
- ends -
---

AT LEIGH ON SEA		DO/VIG

The humble cockle keeps the average Londoner
occupied for, at the most ten minutes, when
purchased by the saucer at the kerb-side- it keeps
the young and old of LEIGH ON SEA, busy however,
all the year round. There are other cockle grounds
around the English coasts, but Leigh claims to be
the biggest.
Leigh's fishing grounds bring out the family
boats in all seasons, and the succulent shell fish
are sieved, washed sorted and boiled, in sheds
down on the shore. The cockles are raked from
the mud at low tide, and the boats are out at the
ground, perhaps for 12 hours at a stretch.

23 SEP 1949
---
"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP    DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world,  Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships.  To their yards and to others
such as Metal Industries, or Arnott and Young's-
come such floating giants as "Rodney", "Revenge",
"Renown"; the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others.  Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes.  Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy, failed
to muzzle, are silent as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive.  Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.
---
COPYRIGHT
FOX
---
PHOTO SHOWS:- Smoke rises in a black pall over the
hull of H.M.S. Rodney, at T. Ward's scrapyard.
Rodney has been broken up in 16 months and the
remaining oil and sludge in her double-bottoms
is burned out to continue the cutting operations.
FOX PHOTOS  MMH
---
Indus - Ship breaking
---
THIS PHOTOGRAPH
has not been submitted
to EVENING PAPERS
---
PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD"
LIBRARY
